claim: On parasol retinal ganglion cells respond nonlinearly to spatial structure in contrast-reversing gratings.
source: As observed previously, responses of both On and Off parasol RGCs showed strong frequency-doubled responses to contrast-reversing gratings (Petrusca et al., 2007; Crook et al., 2008; Cafaro and Rieke, 2013; Figure 1B, right gray box).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work and reference to Figure 1B showing experimental data.

claim: On parasol cells respond weakly to spatial structure in natural inputs.
source: On parasol cells responded weakly to spatial structure in natural inputs (Figure 1D).
evidence: Directly stated and supported by data in Figure 1D.

claim: Off parasol RGCs responded differently to natural and linear-equivalent movies.
source: As reported previously, Off parasol RGCs responded differently to natural and linear-equivalent movies (green and black traces in Figure 1D, right).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 1D and previous work.

claim: On parasol RGCs often showed similar responses to natural and linear-equivalent movies.
source: On parasol RGCs, however, often showed similar responses to natural and linear-equivalent movies (Figure 1D, right; see Turner and Rieke, 2016 for quantification)
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 1D and citation to previous work.

claim: Spatial integration in On parasol responses varied considerably across different naturalistic stimuli.
source: Spatial integration in On parasol responses varied considerably across different naturalistic stimuli, even within the same cell (Turner and Rieke, 2016, Freedland and Rieke, 2021).
evidence: Directly stated and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The NLI for excitatory inputs was significantly larger than that for spike output in On parasol cells responding to image patches.
source: Across cells, however, the NLI for excitatory inputs was significantly larger than that for spike output (Figure 2D; 0.25 ± 0.05 vs 0.08 ± 0.07, mean ± SEM, p < 0.01, n = 10).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical values and reference to Figure 2D.

claim: Nonlinear inhibitory input increased systematically with increasing excitatory NLI.
source: Nonlinear inhibitory input increased systematically with increasing excitatory NLI.
evidence: Directly stated observation from analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Patches that elicited strongly nonlinear excitatory input corresponded to I/E ratios >3.
source: Patches that elicited strongly nonlinear excitatory input, however, corresponded to I/E ratios >3; for these patches inhibitory input is sufficiently large to impact spike output.
evidence: Directly stated observation from analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Inhibitory synaptic input to On parasol RGCs has two distinct components: feedforward and crossover inhibitory input.
source: Inhibitory synaptic input to On parasol RGCs has two distinct components that originate from different retinal circuits (Figure 3A, left; Cafaro and Rieke, 2013; Crook et al., 2014).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 3A and citations to previous work.

claim: Feedforward inhibitory input originates from activity in On retinal pathways and is elicited by increases in light intensity.
source: Feedforward inhibitory input originates from activity in On retinal pathways and, like excitatory input, is elicited by increases in light intensity (Figure 3A, top left).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Crossover inhibitory input originates in Off retinal pathways and is elicited by decreases in light intensity.
source: Crossover inhibitory input originates in Off retinal pathways and is elicited by decreases in light intensity (Figure 3A, bottom left).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Responses in the first cluster had a time course consistent with feedforward inhibitory input and showed linear spatial integration.
source: Responses in the first cluster had a time course consistent with feedforward inhibitory input (see Figure 3A, top right) and showed linear spatial integration – that is responses to image patches and linear-equivalent discs were near identical (Figure 3B, top right).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Responses in the third cluster had a time course consistent with crossover inhibitory input and exhibited strongly nonlinear spatial integration.
source: Responses in the third cluster had a time course consistent with crossover inhibitory input and exhibited strongly nonlinear spatial integration – with much larger responses to images than to the corresponding linear-equivalent discs (Figure 3B, bottom right).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: Crossover inhibitory input alone was sufficient to cancel nonlinear excitatory input.
source: Hence, crossover inhibitory input alone was sufficient to cancel nonlinear excitatory input, and feedforward inhibitory input contributed little to shaping model responses (see also Cafaro and Rieke, 2013).
evidence: Directly stated conclusion from modeling analysis in Figure 4C with citation to previous work.

claim: The offset response exceeded the onset response in each recorded On parasol cell responding to flashed gratings.
source: The offset response exceeded the onset response in each recorded cell (gray points; onset response 0 ± 5 spikes, offset response 57 ± 7 spikes, mean ± SEM, n = 7, p < 0.001).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical values from experimental data.

claim: The I/E ratio was about twofold larger at grating onset than offset.
source: The I/E ratio was about twofold larger at grating onset than offset (Figure 5B, middle; p < 0.01).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical value and reference to Figure 5B.

claim: Excitatory input was delayed relative to inhibitory input at grating onset but not offset.
source: Excitatory input was delayed relative to inhibitory input at grating onset but not offset (Figure 5B, right; onset p < 0.01, offset p = 0.9).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical values and reference to Figure 5B.

claim: The spike response during the first half-cycle of a contrast-reversing grating was substantially smaller than that during subsequent half-cycles.
source: The spike response during the first half-cycle of a contrast-reversing grating was substantially smaller than that during subsequent half-cycles (Figure 5C, left and bottom right).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: The ratio of inhibitory input to excitatory input was substantially larger during the first half-cycle of the grating than during subsequent half-cycles.
source: Similarly, the ratio of inhibitory input to excitatory input was substantially larger during the first half-cycle of the grating than during subsequent half-cycles (Figure 5C, left and top right).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: Off parasol cells exhibited the opposite behavior to On parasol cells, with the smallest I/E ratios and largest spike responses during the first half-cycle of a grating.
source: Off parasol cells exhibited the opposite behavior, with the smallest I/E ratios and largest spike responses during the first half-cycle of a grating (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Measured cone photocurrents to sinusoidal stimuli showed three features: amplitude of cone response was smaller on the first half-cycle than on subsequent cycles, cone responses were asymmetric with larger responses to decrements than increments, and kinetics of cone responses to dark-to-light transitions were sped relative to light-to-dark transitions.
source: Measured cone photocurrents to sinusoidal stimuli showed three features that could potentially shape RGC responses (Figure 6A): (1) the amplitude of the cone response was smaller on the first half-cycle of the grating than on subsequent cycles; (2) cone responses were asymmetric, with larger responses to the dark phase of the grating (decrements) than to bright phase (increments); and, (3) the kinetics of cone responses to dark-to-light transitions were sped relative to responses to light-to-dark transitions.
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 6A showing experimental data.

claim: These properties of the cone responses are created by rapid adaptation in the phototransduction process.
source: These properties of the cone responses are created by rapid adaptation in the phototransduction process (Angueyra et al., 2022), due to a light-dependent increase in PDE activity (Nikonov et al., 2000), which causes the gain of the cone light response to be modulated during each cycle of the sinusoid.
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Models with adapting cones predicted a 70–80% larger I/E ratio on the first grating cycle compared to the steady-state ratio.
source: Models with adapting cones predicted a 70–80% larger I/E ratio on the first grating cycle compared to the steady-state ratio (Figure 6C, top, thin line).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 6C showing model predictions.

claim: This time dependence of the I/E ratio was very similar to that observed in RGC synaptic inputs and was absent in predictions of models with linear cones.
source: This time dependence of the I/E ratio was very similar to that observed in RGC synaptic inputs (closed circles) and was absent in predictions of models with linear cones (thick line).
evidence: Directly stated comparison between model predictions and experimental data.

claim: Models with adapting cones captured the temporal delay between excitatory and inhibitory input.
source: Models with adapting cones also captured the temporal delay between excitatory and inhibitory input (thin lines in Figure 6B; dashed line in Figure 6C, bottom); this delay was again absent for models with linear cones (thick lines in Figure 6B).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figures 6B and 6C showing model predictions.

claim: The transformed stimuli altered cone responses as predicted by the model.
source: Across recorded cones, the transformed stimuli altered cone responses as predicted by the model (Figure 7B).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 7B showing experimental data.

claim: The decrease in I/E ratio observed for the original grating was largely absent for the transformed grating.
source: First, the decrease in I/E ratio observed for the original grating was largely absent for the transformed grating (Figure 7D, top left).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 7D showing experimental data.

claim: The suppression of the spike response at the onset of the original grating stimulus was absent for the transformed stimulus.
source: Second, the suppression of the spike response at the onset of the original grating stimulus was absent for the transformed stimulus (Figure 7D, bottom left).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 7D showing experimental data.

claim: Excitatory inputs in response to the transformed stimuli were substantially delayed compared to excitatory inputs in response to the original stimuli.
source: Excitatory inputs in response to the transformed stimuli were substantially delayed compared to excitatory inputs in response to the original stimuli (Figure 7D, middle).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 7D showing experimental data.

claim: The substantial phase shift between excitatory and inhibitory input observed for conventional gratings was almost entirely eliminated by the transformed gratings.
source: This shift in timing of excitatory input caused it to overlap more with inhibitory input, and the substantial phase shift between excitatory and inhibitory input observed for conventional gratings was almost entirely eliminated by the transformed gratings (Figure 7D, right).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 7D showing experimental data.

claim: Cone adaptation can explain the majority of the observed time dependence of the On parasol responses to contrast-reversing gratings.
source: The combination of modeling in Figure 6 and direct manipulation of the cone responses in Figure 7 indicate that cone adaptation can explain the majority of the observed time dependence of the On parasol responses to contrast-reversing gratings.
evidence: Directly stated conclusion from combined modeling and experimental results.

claim: Adaptation substantially attenuated the amplitude of modeled cone responses compared to responses of cones without adaptation.
source: Adaptation substantially attenuated the amplitude of modeled cone responses compared to responses of cones without adaptation (Figure 8A, bottom).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 8A showing model predictions.

claim: I/E ratios varied widely across time bins, but were systematically larger for models with adapting cones compared to models with nonadapting cones.
source: I/E ratios varied widely across time bins, but were systematically larger for models with adapting cones compared to models with nonadapting cones (Figure 8B).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 8B showing model predictions.

claim: Cone adaptation substantially increased the number of patches in which inhibitory input was sufficiently large to attenuate excitatory input.
source: Cone adaptation substantially increased the number of patches in which inhibitory input was sufficiently large to attenuate excitatory input (I/E ratios exceeding 3).
evidence: Directly stated conclusion from analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Image patches with positive local luminance and high spatial contrast should activate both On and Off parasol cells when On parasol RGCs exhibit near-linear spatial integration and Off parasol RGCs show nonlinear integration.
source: Our results suggest that On parasol RGCs exhibit near-linear spatial integration (i.e., top left in Figure 9A) while Off parasol RGCs show nonlinear integration (bottom right). In this case, image patches with positive local luminance and high spatial contrast should activate both On and Off parasol cells; such coactivation would be absent if both cells exhibited linear spatial integration.
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 9A showing model predictions.

claim: The joint responses of On and Off cells should permit discrimination of image patches with small differences in local luminance and/or spatial contrast.
source: This means that the joint responses of On and Off cells should permit discrimination of image patches with small differences in local luminance and/or spatial contrast (Figure 9—figure supplement 1); such discrimination is not possible from responses of either cell type considered alone.
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 9—figure supplement 1 showing model predictions.

claim: The linear On/nonlinear Off combination provides better discrimination than a nonlinear On/linear Off combination.
source: Furthermore, the linear On/nonlinear Off combination provides better discrimination than a nonlinear On/linear Off combination (Figure 9—figure supplement 1) due to the stronger Off responses to spatial structure (Figure 9A).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 9—figure supplement 1 and Figure 9A showing model predictions.

claim: Inhibitory input contributes minimally to On parasol spike responses to spatially uniform stimuli.
source: Inhibitory synaptic input contributes minimally to On parasol spike responses to spatially uniform stimuli (Cafaro and Rieke, 2013).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to previous work.

claim: Nonlinear spatial integration is weak or absent at the onset of a grating because inhibitory input is large compared to excitatory input and the two overlap in time.
source: Nonlinear spatial integration is weak or absent at the onset of a grating because inhibitory input is large compared to excitatory input and the two overlap in time.
evidence: Directly stated conclusion from analyses in Figure 5.

claim: Nonlinear spatial integration increases for later cycles of a periodic grating stimulus, due to a decrease in the I/E ratio and a delay of inhibitory input relative to excitatory input.
source: Nonlinear spatial integration increases for later cycles of a periodic grating stimulus, due to a decrease in the I/E ratio and a delay of inhibitory input relative to excitatory input.
evidence: Directly stated conclusion from analyses in Figure 5.

claim: Nonlinear spatial integration in excitatory synaptic input is typically generated by rectifying nonlinearities at the bipolar output synapse.
source: Nonlinear spatial integration in excitatory synaptic input is typically generated by rectifying nonlinearities at the bipolar output synapse (Demb et al., 1999; Demb et al., 2001; Borghuis et al., 2013; but see Schreyer and Gollisch, 2021).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Linearity of the spike response requires that nonlinear subunits for excitatory and inhibitory circuits have similar sizes.
source: This analysis suggests that linearity of the spike response requires that nonlinear subunits for excitatory and inhibitory circuits have similar sizes.
evidence: Directly stated conclusion from modeling analysis in Figure 4D.

claim: The insensitivity of the On parasol spike response to spatial structure in natural inputs depends on nonlinear crossover inhibitory input that has a similar spatial scale as nonlinear excitatory input and exhibits strong nonlinear spatial integration.
source: In summary, the modeling of Figure 4 indicates that the insensitivity of the On parasol spike response to spatial structure in natural inputs depends on nonlinear crossover inhibitory input that has a similar spatial scale as nonlinear excitatory input and exhibits strong nonlinear spatial integration.
evidence: Directly stated conclusion from modeling analysis in Figure 4.

claim: Off retinal circuits are the main source of the inhibitory input that regulates spatial integration.
source: Importantly for the analyses below, this means that Off retinal circuits are the main source of the inhibitory input that regulates spatial integration.
evidence: Directly stated conclusion from modeling analysis in Figure 4.

claim: Parasol RGC responses do not appear to be shaped by synaptic depression in the experiments.
source: Parasol RGC responses, however, do not appear to be similarly shaped by synaptic depression in our experiments.
evidence: Directly stated conclusion from experimental observations.

claim: The onset of a spatially uniform light step from a constant background elicited large excitatory input and strong spike responses in both On and Off parasol cells.
source: The onset of a spatially uniform light step from a constant background elicited large excitatory input and strong spike responses in both On and Off parasol cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; see also Turner and Rieke, 2016), indicating that at the mean luminance levels used here, bipolar cells upstream of parasol RGCs have vesicles available to produce strong synaptic output.
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and citation to previous work.

claim: Synaptic depression in upstream bipolar cells is not likely to play a major role in the asymmetry seen at the onset of a periodic grating stimulus.
source: Thus, synaptic depression in upstream bipolar cells is not likely to play a major role in the asymmetry seen at the onset of a periodic grating stimulus (e.g., Figure 1).
evidence: Directly stated conclusion from experimental observations.

claim: Rapid cone adaptation limits the amplitude of the increase in excitatory input at grating onset.
source: Rapid cone adaptation (time constant <100 ms) limits the amplitude of the increase in excitatory input at grating onset (compare thick and thin lines in Figure 6B).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 6B showing model predictions.

claim: For subsequent cycles of the grating, cones encountering an increase in light intensity start from a higher signaling gain and respond more quickly than cones encountering a decrease in light intensity.
source: Hence, for subsequent cycles of the grating, cones encountering an increase in light intensity start from a higher signaling gain and respond more quickly than cones encountering a decrease in light intensity.
evidence: Directly stated explanation of model behavior.

claim: This increases the amplitude of excitatory input relative to inhibitory input, and creates a time window in which excitatory input increases before inhibitory input.
source: This increases the amplitude of excitatory input relative to inhibitory input, and creates a time window in which excitatory input increases before inhibitory input.
evidence: Directly stated explanation of model behavior.

claim: Without adaptation (i.e., with linear cones), this shift in amplitude and timing of excitatory input relative to inhibitory input does not occur.
source: Without adaptation (i.e., with linear cones), this shift in amplitude and timing of excitatory input relative to inhibitory input does not occur.
evidence: Directly stated conclusion from model comparison.

claim: Cone adaptation shifted the I/E balance in favor of inhibitory input for naturalistic inputs, which decreased the sensitivity of On parasol RGC responses to spatial structure.
source: Specifically, adaptation in the cones shifted the I/E balance in favor of inhibitory input, and this in turn decreased the sensitivity of On parasol RGC responses to spatial structure.
evidence: Directly stated conclusion from modeling analysis in Figures 6 and 8.

claim: Corresponding On and Off RGCs can exhibit asymmetries in addition to the polarity of their responses.
source: Multiple findings show that this picture is too simple, and in fact that corresponding On and Off RGCs can exhibit asymmetries in addition to the polarity of their responses. This includes differences in receptive field size (Balasubramanian and Sterling, 2009), contrast sensitivity (Zaghloul et al., 2003), rectification (Turner and Rieke, 2016), and balance of excitatory and inhibitory inputs (Murphy and Rieke, 2006).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Some asymmetries between On and Off RGCs have been suggested to be important in population coding of natural inputs.
source: Some of these asymmetries – for example the smaller receptive fields of Off RGCs – have been suggested to be important in population coding of natural inputs (Balasubramanian and Sterling, 2009; Ratliff et al., 2010; Pandarinath et al., 2010; Karklin and Simoncelli, 2011).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous work.

claim: On/Off asymmetries differ for different RGC types.
source: On/Off asymmetries also differ for different RGC types (Ravi et al., 2018), a factor that will need to be considered in efficient coding arguments.
evidence: Directly stated with citation to previous work.

claim: On and Off parasol RGCs both exhibit nonlinear spatial integration in response to contrast-reversing gratings.
source: On and Off parasol RGCs both exhibit nonlinear spatial integration in response to contrast-reversing gratings (Petrusca et al., 2007; Crook et al., 2008).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Off parasol RGCs respond nonlinearly to spatial structure in natural images.
source: Off parasol RGCs similarly respond nonlinearly to spatial structure in natural images, but unexpectedly On parasol RGCs respond near linearly.
evidence: Directly stated observation from experimental data.

claim: Certain image features may be distinguishable based on the joint activity of pairs of On and Off cells even when the responses of the individual cells are ambiguous.
source: The difference in sensitivity to spatial structure in natural images suggests that certain features – specifically image patches that have similar positive luminance and differences in spatial contrast – may be distinguishable based on the joint activity of pairs of On and Off cells even when the responses of the individual cells are ambiguous.
evidence: Directly stated conclusion from modeling analysis in Figure 9.

claim: Macaque retinas were obtained through the Tissue Distribution Program of the Regional Primate Research Center at the University of Washington.
source: In brief, macaque retinas (Macaca fascicularis, Macaca nemistrina, and Macaca mulatta) were obtained through the Tissue Distribution Program of the Regional Primate Research Center at the University of Washington.
evidence: Directly stated in Materials and methods section.

claim: Pieces of retina attached to the pigment epithelium were stored in ~32–34°C oxygenated Ames medium and dark adapted for >1 hr.
source: Pieces of retina attached to the pigment epithelium were stored in ∼32–34°C oxygenated (95% O2/5% CO2) Ames medium (Sigma, St Louis, MO) and dark adapted for >1 hr.
evidence: Directly stated in Materials and methods section.

claim: Parasol RGCs were targeted for electrical recordings based on their characteristic soma size and response to a light step.
source: Parasol RGCs were targeted for electrical recordings based on their characteristic soma size and response to a light step.
evidence: Directly stated in Materials and methods section.

claim: Mean light levels produced 4000 isomerizations (R*)/M or L-cone/s, 1000 R*/S-cone/s, and 9000 R*/rod/s.
source: Unless otherwise noted, mean light levels produced 4000 isomerizations (R*)/M or L-cone/s, 1000 R*/S-cone/s, and 9000 R*/rod/s; this corresponds to 3x10-12 sugar-cube inches/rod/s (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_Baylor).
evidence: Directly stated in Materials and methods section.

claim: The average spatial contrast of the image patches probed was 0.3, and many patches had spatial contrasts exceeding 0.5.
source: The average spatial contrast of the image patches probed was 0.3, and many patches had spatial contrasts exceeding 0.5.
evidence: Directly stated in Materials and methods section.

claim: The cone responses are well captured by an empirically derived biophysical model of cone phototransduction.
source: The cone responses are well captured by an empirically derived biophysical model of cone phototransduction (see Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Materials and methods and Angueyra et al., 2022 for details).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and citation to previous work.

claim: All parameters of the cone model were set by previous measurements.
source: All parameters of the cone model were set by previous measurements.
evidence: Directly stated in Materials and methods section.

claim: 60–70% of the preparations met the retina sensitivity criterion.
source: 60–70% of the preparations met this criterion.
evidence: Directly stated in Materials and methods section.
